title: General Surgery Diploma — Lower Limb: Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics MCQ Bank (96 Questions)

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which structure divides the greater sciatic foramen into superior and inferior compartments?
questions.explanation: The piriformis muscle passes through the greater sciatic foramen, dividing it into suprapiriform and infrapiriform compartments.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which neurovascular structures emerge ABOVE the piriformis muscle through the greater sciatic foramen?
questions.explanation: The superior gluteal nerve and vessels are the sole neurovascular structures passing through the greater sciatic foramen above the piriformis.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which structures exit the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, cross the ischial spine, and re-enter via the lesser sciatic foramen?
options: Sciatic nerve and posterior femoral cutaneous nerve
Pudendal nerve and nerve to obturator internus (with internal pudendal vessels)
Nerve to quadratus femoris and inferior gluteal vessels
questions.explanation: The pudendal nerve, internal pudendal vessels, and nerve to obturator internus exit below piriformis, hook around the ischial spine/sacrospinous ligament, and enter the perineum via the lesser sciatic foramen.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Where is the safe site for an intramuscular injection in the gluteal region to avoid sciatic nerve injury?
questions.explanation: The upper outer quadrant is safely away from the sciatic nerve and superior/inferior gluteal neurovascular bundles.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Injury to the superior gluteal nerve results in paralysis of gluteus medius and minimus, leading clinically to:
options: Loss of hip extension when climbing stairs
Positive Trendelenburg sign (pelvis sags on the unsupported contralateral side)
Loss of sensation over the lateral thigh
questions.explanation: Gluteus medius and minimus abduct the hip and stabilize the pelvis during single-leg stance; paralysis causes a positive Trendelenburg sign.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which nerve supplies the gluteus maximus muscle?
questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus is solely innervated by the inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which cutaneous nerve supplies the skin of the lower lateral quadrant of the buttock and the lateral aspect of the thigh down to the knee?
options: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (L2, L3)
questions.explanation: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (L2, L3) passes behind the lateral end of the inguinal ligament and supplies the lateral thigh and lower lateral buttock.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Entrapment of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh beneath the inguinal ligament causes a painful dysesthesia known as:
questions.explanation: Compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve near the ASIS/inguinal ligament produces burning pain and numbness over the anterolateral thigh (meralgia paresthetica).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which cutaneous nerve supplies the skin immediately below the middle part of the inguinal ligament (over the femoral triangle)?
options: Femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2)
Lateral cutaneous branch of subcostal nerve (T12)
questions.explanation: The femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve enters behind the middle of the inguinal ligament to supply skin over the femoral triangle.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: The patellar plexus of cutaneous nerves lying in front of the knee joint is formed by all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Intermediate and medial cutaneous nerves of thigh
questions.explanation: The patellar plexus is formed anteriorly by the infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve and the lateral, intermediate, and medial cutaneous nerves of the thigh.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which cutaneous nerve supplies the skin of the posterior aspect of the thigh, popliteal fossa, and lower buttock?
options: Posterior femoral cutaneous nerve (S1, S2, S3)
questions.explanation: The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve arises from the sacral plexus (S1-S3) and runs down the back of the thigh beneath fascia lata.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: What spinal segments contribute to the obturator nerve?
options: Dorsal divisions of L2, L3, L4
Ventral divisions of L2, L3, L4
questions.explanation: The obturator nerve arises from the anterior (ventral) divisions of L2, L3, and L4 of the lumbar plexus, whereas the femoral nerve arises from the dorsal divisions.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which muscle exits the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen?
questions.explanation: The tendon of obturator internus turns sharply around the lesser sciatic notch/ischial spine to exit via the lesser sciatic foramen.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which nerve supplies both the obturator internus and superior gemellus muscles?
options: Nerve to obturator internus (L5, S1, S2)
questions.explanation: The nerve to obturator internus innervates obturator internus and the superior gemellus, whereas the nerve to quadratus femoris innervates quadratus femoris and inferior gemellus.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Why does fusion of the membranous layer of superficial fascia (Scarpa's/Colles' fascia) to the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament hold clinical importance?
options: It prevents extravasated urine in anterior urethral rupture from tracking down into the thigh
It anchors the great saphenous vein
questions.explanation: The attachment of Colles' fascia to the fascia lata along Holden's line prevents urine from descending into the thigh following bulbar urethral rupture.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Where is the dorsal venous arch of the foot located?
options: Over the heads of the metatarsal bones
questions.explanation: The dorsal venous arch lies in the subcutaneous tissue over the heads of the metatarsals and gives rise to the great and small saphenous veins.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: The great (long) saphenous vein originates from the medial end of the dorsal venous arch and ascends:
questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein passes directly in front of the medial malleolus (accompanied by the saphenous nerve), making this the classic anatomical landmark for emergency venous cutdown.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Where does the great saphenous vein terminate?
options: Into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa
Into the femoral vein through the saphenous opening, ~4 cm below and lateral to the pubic tubercle
Directly into the external iliac vein above the inguinal ligament
questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein pierces the cribriform fascia at the saphenous hiatus (~4 cm inferolateral to the pubic tubercle) to join the femoral vein.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which tributary of the great saphenous vein anastomoses with the lateral thoracic vein to form the thoracoepigastric vein (a caval-caval shunt)?
questions.explanation: The superficial epigastric vein communicates with the lateral thoracic vein, forming an important collateral pathway between the IVC and SVC.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: What is the anatomical course and termination of the small (short) saphenous vein?
options: Ascends anterior to medial malleolus and drains into femoral vein
Ascends posterior to lateral malleolus and drains into the popliteal vein
Ascends along the lateral thigh into the superior gluteal vein
Drains directly into the anterior tibial vein
questions.explanation: The small saphenous vein arises from the lateral dorsal venous arch, passes behind the lateral malleolus (with the sural nerve), and pierces the popliteal fascia to enter the popliteal vein.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Why do varicose veins develop when valves in the perforating veins become incompetent?
options: Blood flows from superficial to deep veins too rapidly
High-pressure blood from deep veins is pumped retrograde into superficial veins during calf muscle contraction
Arterial blood shunts directly into the dorsal venous arch
Lymphatic obstruction dilates the deep veins
questions.explanation: Normal perforator valves direct blood from superficial to deep veins; valvular incompetence allows high-pressure deep venous blood to reflux into the unsupported superficial veins.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which nerve is most at risk of injury during harvesting or stripping of the great saphenous vein in the lower leg?
questions.explanation: The saphenous nerve accompanies the great saphenous vein along the medial leg and anterior to the medial malleolus.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: The medial members of the horizontal group of superficial inguinal lymph nodes receive lymph from all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Anterior abdominal wall below the umbilicus
Lower half of the anal canal
questions.explanation: The testis drains directly along the testicular vessels to the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes, bypassing the inguinal nodes completely.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: The lateral members of the horizontal group of superficial inguinal lymph nodes drain lymph from:
options: The back below the level of the iliac crest
The upper half of the anal canal
The anterior abdominal wall above the umbilicus
questions.explanation: Lateral horizontal superficial inguinal nodes drain the gluteal region and back below the iliac crest.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: The vertical group of superficial inguinal lymph nodes lies along the termination of the great saphenous vein and receives lymph primarily from:
options: The anteromedial superficial lymphatics of the lower limb
The posterolateral superficial lymphatics along the small saphenous vein
The deep structures of the foot
questions.explanation: Superficial lymphatics accompanying the great saphenous vein drain into the vertical group of superficial inguinal nodes.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Where do the deep inguinal lymph nodes lie, and through which opening do their efferents pass to the external iliac nodes?
options: Lateral to femoral artery; pass through adductor canal
Medial to femoral vein under fascia lata; pass through the femoral canal/ring
Inside the popliteal fossa; pass through obturator canal
Superficial to cribriform fascia; pass through saphenous hiatus
questions.explanation: Deep inguinal nodes (1–3 nodes) lie along the medial side of the femoral vein and drain upwards through the femoral canal into external iliac nodes.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Cloquet’s (Rosenmüller’s) lymph node is the highest deep inguinal node located in the femoral canal and specifically receives direct lymph from:
options: The heel and lateral border of the foot
questions.explanation: Cloquet's node lies within the femoral ring and drains the glans penis/clitoris as well as deep inguinal afferents.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which lymph nodes receive superficial lymphatics running alongside the small saphenous vein from the lateral foot and posterolateral leg?
questions.explanation: Superficial lymphatics along the small saphenous vein drain first into the popliteal lymph nodes embedded in the popliteal fossa fat.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: How do efferent lymphatic vessels from the popliteal lymph nodes reach the deep inguinal lymph nodes?
options: Ascending through the adductor hiatus and adductor canal accompanying the femoral vessels
questions.explanation: Efferents from popliteal nodes travel upwards with the popliteal and femoral vessels through the adductor canal to reach the deep inguinal nodes.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: How many lymph nodes typically constitute the popliteal group?
questions.explanation: Approximately 6 small popliteal lymph nodes lie embedded in the fatty tissue around the popliteal vessels.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: An infection on the lateral border of the heel is most likely to cause tender lymphadenopathy initially in which group?
questions.explanation: Lymph from the lateral foot/heel tracks along the small saphenous vein directly to the popliteal lymph nodes.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which superficial arteries accompany the superficial veins in the groin and arise from the femoral artery?
options: Superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, and internal pudendal arteries
Superficial circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric, and superficial external pudendal arteries
Medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries
Descending genicular and profunda femoris arteries
questions.explanation: The femoral artery gives off three superficial branches just below the inguinal ligament: superficial circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric, and superficial external pudendal.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which structures are enclosed within the femoral sheath?
options: Femoral nerve, femoral artery, and femoral vein
Femoral artery, femoral vein, and femoral canal (containing deep inguinal lymphatics)
Femoral artery and femoral nerve only
Great saphenous vein and femoral nerve
questions.explanation: The femoral sheath encloses the femoral artery (lateral compartment), femoral vein (intermediate compartment), and femoral canal (medial compartment). The femoral nerve lies outside the sheath.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: From which fascial layers of the abdomen is the femoral sheath derived?
options: External oblique aponeurosis anteriorly and internal oblique posteriorly
Fascia transversalis anteriorly and fascia iliaca posteriorly
Scarpa's fascia anteriorly and pectineal fascia posteriorly
Peritoneum anteriorly and obturator fascia posteriorly
questions.explanation: The femoral sheath is a downward prolongation of fascia transversalis anteriorly and fascia iliaca posteriorly for about 1 inch (2.5–4 cm) below the inguinal ligament.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: What are the exact anatomical boundaries of the femoral ring (the upper abdominal opening of the femoral canal)?
options: Anteriorly: inguinal ligament; Posteriorly: pectineal ligament; Medially: lacunar ligament; Laterally: femoral vein
Anteriorly: fascia lata; Posteriorly: psoas major; Medially: femoral artery; Laterally: sartorius
Anteriorly: conjoint tendon; Posteriorly: pubic symphysis; Medially: femoral vein; Laterally: lacunar ligament
Anteriorly: sartorius; Posteriorly: adductor longus; Medially: gracilis; Laterally: pectineus
questions.explanation: The femoral ring is bounded anteriorly by the inguinal ligament, posteriorly by Astley Cooper's pectineal ligament, medially by Gimbernat's lacunar ligament, and laterally by the femoral vein.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Why are femoral hernias particularly prone to strangulation?
options: Because the femoral nerve compresses the sac
Because the femoral ring is small and bounded by rigid, unyielding structures (especially the sharp medial edge of the lacunar ligament)
Because they always contain the urinary bladder
Because the femoral artery pulsates against the neck
questions.explanation: The tight, rigid margins of the femoral ring—particularly the sharp lacunar ligament medially—make femoral hernias highly susceptible to irreducibility and strangulation.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Where is the neck of a femoral hernia sac located relative to the pubic tubercle?
options: Above and medial to the pubic tubercle
Below and lateral to the pubic tubercle
Above and lateral to the pubic tubercle
questions.explanation: Femoral hernias emerge through the saphenous opening below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, whereas inguinal hernias emerge above and medial to it.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which structure forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle?
questions.explanation: The femoral triangle is bounded superiorly by the inguinal ligament, laterally by the medial border of sartorius, and medially by the medial border of adductor longus.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which muscles form the floor (posterior wall) of the femoral triangle from lateral to medial?
options: Iliacus, psoas major, pectineus, and adductor longus
Vastus medialis, rectus femoris, and gracilis
Sartorius, tensor fasciae latae, and obturator externus
questions.explanation: From lateral to medial, the gutter-shaped floor of the femoral triangle is formed by iliacus, psoas major, pectineus, and adductor longus.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Where does the adductor (Hunter's / subsartorial) canal begin and end?
options: Begins at the inguinal ligament and ends at the apex of the femoral triangle
Begins at the apex of the femoral triangle and ends at the adductor hiatus in adductor magnus
Begins at the greater sciatic foramen and ends at the knee joint
Begins at the saphenous opening and ends at the medial malleolus
questions.explanation: The adductor canal extends through the middle third of the medial thigh from the apex of the femoral triangle to the adductor hiatus.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a content of the adductor (Hunter's) canal?
questions.explanation: The femoral nerve divides in the femoral triangle; only its saphenous branch and nerve to vastus medialis enter the adductor canal alongside the femoral vessels.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which structures pass through the adductor hiatus into the popliteal fossa?
options: Femoral artery, femoral vein, posterior division of obturator nerve, and deep lymphatics
Great saphenous vein and saphenous nerve
questions.explanation: The femoral artery and vein pass through the adductor hiatus to become the popliteal vessels, accompanied by the genicular branch of the posterior obturator nerve and lymphatics.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: What forms the superolateral and superomedial boundaries of the popliteal fossa?
options: Superolateral: biceps femoris; Superomedial: semitendinosus and semimembranosus
Superolateral: lateral head of gastrocnemius; Superomedial: medial head of gastrocnemius
questions.explanation: The diamond-shaped popliteal fossa is bounded superolaterally by biceps femoris, superomedially by semimembranosus/semitendinosus, and inferiorly by the two heads of gastrocnemius.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: What forms the floor (anterior wall) of the popliteal fossa from above downwards?
options: Popliteal surface of femur, oblique popliteal ligament (knee capsule), and fascia covering popliteus muscle
Posterior surface of tibia and fibula only
questions.explanation: The deep floor of the popliteal fossa consists superiorly of the popliteal surface of the femur, centrally of the posterior knee capsule/oblique popliteal ligament, and inferiorly of the popliteus muscle.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: What is the arrangement of the major neurovascular structures in the popliteal fossa from superficial (posterior) to deep (anterior)?
options: Popliteal artery → Popliteal vein → Tibial nerve
Tibial nerve → Popliteal vein → Popliteal artery
Popliteal vein → Tibial nerve → Popliteal artery
Common peroneal nerve → Popliteal artery → Popliteal vein
questions.explanation: From superficial (posterior) to deep (anterior) inside the popliteal fossa, the order is Tibial Nerve, Popliteal Vein, and Popliteal Artery (deepest, directly against the femur/capsule).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: How does the anatomical relationship between the popliteal artery and popliteal vein change as they descend through the popliteal fossa?
options: The artery stays strictly medial throughout
The artery runs Medial → Deep → Lateral (M.D.L.) relative to the vein, while the vein runs Medial → Superficial → Lateral (M.S.L.)
The vein stays strictly posterior to the artery
They do not cross each other
questions.explanation: In the upper fossa, the vein is lateral to the artery; in the middle, superficial/posterior to it; and distally, medial to it (making the artery Medial, Deep, then Lateral relative to the vein).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which nerve winds around the lateral aspect of the neck of the fibula, making it highly vulnerable to fracture or tight plaster casts?
questions.explanation: The common peroneal nerve leaves the popliteal fossa along the medial border of biceps femoris and wraps superficially around the neck of the fibula.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: At which exact anatomical landmark does the femoral artery begin?
options: Midinguinal point (halfway between ASIS and pubic symphysis)
questions.explanation: The external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery behind the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point (halfway between the ASIS and the symphysis pubis).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Where does the profunda femoris (deep artery of the thigh) arise from the femoral artery?
options: From the posterolateral aspect of the femoral artery ~4 cm (1.5 inches) below the inguinal ligament
questions.explanation: The profunda femoris arises from the posterolateral side of the femoral artery roughly 4 cm below the inguinal ligament and supplies the thigh compartments via circumflex and perforating branches.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Where does the popliteal artery terminate by dividing into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries?
options: At the lower border of the popliteus muscle
At the neck of the fibula
questions.explanation: The popliteal artery ends at the lower border of the popliteus muscle by bifurcating into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which arteries participate in the trochanteric anastomosis around the neck of the femur?
options: Superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, medial circumflex femoral, and lateral circumflex femoral arteries
Obturator and internal pudendal arteries only
questions.explanation: The trochanteric anastomosis is formed by the superior and inferior gluteal arteries anastomosing with ascending branches of the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries; it provides the main blood supply to the femoral head.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Why is an intracapsular fracture of the femoral neck associated with a high risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head?
options: It tears the retinacular vessels derived from the medial circumflex femoral artery (trochanteric anastomosis)
questions.explanation: The femoral head depends predominantly on retinacular branches from the medial circumflex femoral artery traveling along the femoral neck capsule.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which arteries form the cruciate anastomosis at the level of the lesser trochanter (providing collateral flow if the femoral artery is occluded)?
options: Inferior gluteal, transverse branches of medial & lateral circumflex femoral, and 1st perforating artery of profunda femoris
Superior gluteal and internal pudendal arteries
questions.explanation: The cruciate anastomosis connects the internal iliac system (inferior gluteal) with the profunda femoris system (medial/lateral circumflex femoral and 1st perforating arteries).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: How does the anterior tibial artery enter the anterior compartment of the leg?
options: By passing through the adductor hiatus
By passing forward through an opening in the upper part of the interosseous membrane
By passing behind the lateral malleolus
questions.explanation: Arising at the lower border of popliteus, the anterior tibial artery passes anteriorly above the upper margin of the interosseous membrane into the anterior leg compartment.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: At what landmark does the anterior tibial artery continue as the dorsalis pedis artery?
options: Midway between the medial and lateral malleoli in front of the ankle joint
At the base of the 5th metatarsal
questions.explanation: In front of the ankle joint, midway between the two malleoli, the anterior tibial artery becomes the dorsalis pedis artery (palpable just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: What is the largest branch of the posterior tibial artery, which runs in the posterior compartment near the fibula?
questions.explanation: The peroneal (fibular) artery arises from the posterior tibial artery ~2.5 cm below popliteus and descends along the fibula, giving a perforating branch to the ankle.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Where does the posterior tibial artery terminate by dividing into the medial and lateral plantar arteries?
options: Deep to the flexor retinaculum (behind the medial malleolus)
In front of the ankle joint
At the lower border of popliteus
At the neck of the fibula
questions.explanation: The posterior tibial artery passes behind the medial malleolus deep to the flexor retinaculum and divides into medial and lateral plantar arteries.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: What is the exact order of structures passing behind the medial malleolus deep to the flexor retinaculum from anteromedial to posterolateral ('Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry')?
options: Tibialis posterior, Flexor digitorum longus, Posterior tibial artery & veins, Tibial nerve, Flexor hallucis longus
Tibialis anterior, Extensor hallucis longus, Anterior tibial artery, Deep peroneal nerve
Peroneus longus, Peroneus brevis, Sural nerve, Small saphenous vein
Flexor hallucis longus, Tibial nerve, Posterior tibial artery, Tibialis posterior
questions.explanation: From medial/anterior to lateral/posterior under the flexor retinaculum: Tibialis posterior tendon, Flexor digitorum longus tendon, Posterior tibial vessels, Tibial nerve, and Flexor hallucis longus tendon.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which artery completes the deep plantar arch on the sole of the foot by joining the lateral plantar artery?
options: Deep plantar branch of the dorsalis pedis artery (entering via the 1st intermetatarsal space)
questions.explanation: The deep plantar branch of the dorsalis pedis dives between the two heads of the 1st dorsal interosseous muscle to anastomose with the lateral plantar artery, completing the deep plantar arch.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which nerve accompanies the anterior tibial artery in the anterior compartment of the leg?
questions.explanation: The deep peroneal nerve descends along the anterior surface of the interosseous membrane alongside the anterior tibial artery.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: What is the cutaneous sensory distribution of the deep peroneal nerve?
options: Skin of the entire dorsum of the foot
Skin of the adjacent sides (web space) of the 1st and 2nd toes
Medial malleolus and medial border of the foot
questions.explanation: The deep peroneal nerve supplies all muscles of the anterior leg compartment and terminates cutaneously in the first dorsal web space (between the 1st and 2nd toes).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which muscles are innervated by the superficial peroneal (musculocutaneous) nerve?
options: Tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus
Tibialis posterior and flexor digitorum longus
questions.explanation: The superficial peroneal nerve innervates the lateral compartment muscles (peroneus longus and brevis—foot evertors) and supplies skin over the lower anterolateral leg and most of the dorsum of the foot.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Injury to the common peroneal nerve at the neck of the fibula produces which characteristic clinical presentation?
options: Foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion and eversion, resulting in equinovarus posture and high-stepping gait) plus sensory loss over the anterolateral leg and dorsum of foot
Inability to flex the toes only
questions.explanation: Common peroneal nerve palsy paralyzes both the anterior (dorsiflexors) and lateral (evertors) compartments, causing unopposed plantarflexion and inversion (foot drop).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Injury to the tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa or upper leg results in which foot deformity?
options: Calcaneovalgus (unopposed dorsiflexion and eversion due to paralysis of plantarflexors and invertors) with sensory loss on the sole
Loss of sensation in the 1st web space
questions.explanation: Tibial nerve paralysis eliminates plantarflexion (gastrocnemius/soleus) and inversion (tibialis posterior), leaving the foot pulled into dorsiflexion and eversion (calcaneovalgus).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: How does the tibial nerve change its relationship to the posterior tibial artery as it descends in the posterior compartment of the leg?
options: Runs Medial → Superficial (posterior) → Lateral (M.S.L.) relative to the artery
questions.explanation: The tibial nerve enters the leg medial to the posterior tibial artery, crosses posterior (superficial) to it, and lies lateral to the artery at the ankle.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which nerve supplies the skin of the posterolateral lower leg and the lateral border of the foot up to the little toe?
questions.explanation: The sural nerve (formed by medial sural cutaneous branch of tibial nerve and sural communicating branch of common peroneal nerve) descends with the small saphenous vein to supply the lateral foot.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: The medial plantar nerve supplies cutaneous sensation to which area of the sole of the foot (analogous to the median nerve in the hand)?
questions.explanation: Just like the median nerve in the hand, the medial plantar nerve supplies the medial 3½ toes and innervates abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, flexor hallucis brevis, and the 1st lumbrical.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: The lateral plantar nerve supplies cutaneous sensation to which area of the sole of the foot (analogous to the ulnar nerve in the hand)?
options: Lateral 1½ digits (5th toe and lateral half of 4th toe) and most deep intrinsic muscles of the foot
questions.explanation: Analogous to the ulnar nerve in the hand, the lateral plantar nerve supplies the lateral 1½ digits and all interossei, adductor hallucis, lateral 3 lumbricals, and quadratus plantae.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which nerve supplies the skin over the medial side of the heel (heel pad)?
options: Medial calcaneal branches of the tibial nerve
questions.explanation: Medial calcaneal branches arise directly from the tibial nerve proximal to its bifurcation to supply the skin of the heel.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: How far distally does the saphenous nerve provide cutaneous innervation?
options: Down to the knee joint only
Down the medial leg, anterior to the medial malleolus, along the medial border of the foot up to the ball of the big toe (1st MTP joint)
To the tip of the 5th toe
To the sole of the heel
questions.explanation: The saphenous nerve is the longest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve, extending along the medial foot as far as the head of the 1st metatarsal.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which nerve is exclusively motor and supplies the adductor muscles of the thigh (except the hamstring part of adductor magnus) plus gracilis and obturator externus?
questions.explanation: The obturator nerve innervates the medial (adductor) compartment of the thigh and sends a cutaneous branch to the medial thigh and an articular branch to the hip and knee.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Why can hip joint pathology (such as osteoarthritis or Perthes disease) present clinically as referred pain to the medial side of the knee?
options: Shared innervation via the obturator nerve (which supplies both the hip joint and the knee joint/medial thigh)
questions.explanation: The obturator nerve supplies articular branches to both the hip and knee joints as well as cutaneous sensation to the medial thigh, explaining referred knee pain in hip disease.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which muscle of the thigh has a dual nerve supply from both the obturator nerve and the tibial division of the sciatic nerve?
questions.explanation: The adductor portion of adductor magnus is innervated by the posterior division of the obturator nerve, while its hamstring portion (attaching to the adductor tubercle) is innervated by the tibial nerve.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which muscle in the anterior thigh has a dual nerve supply from the femoral nerve and the obturator nerve?
questions.explanation: Pectineus is innervated primarily by the femoral nerve and frequently receives an accessory branch from the obturator nerve.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which muscle in the posterior thigh has a dual nerve supply from the tibial and common peroneal divisions of the sciatic nerve?
options: Biceps femoris (long head by tibial nerve; short head by common peroneal nerve)
questions.explanation: The long head of biceps femoris is supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve, whereas the short head is supplied by the common peroneal division.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: What is the mechanism of the 'calf muscle pump' in venous return of the lower limb?
options: Contraction of gastrocnemius and soleus compresses the deep venae comitantes within the tight deep fascia (crural fascia), propelling blood upward while valves prevent reflux
Arterial pulsations push blood down the saphenous veins
Negative pressure in the popliteal fossa draws blood from the femoral vein
questions.explanation: During walking, contraction of the calf muscles within the unyielding deep fascia squeezes blood centrally through valved deep veins and draws blood inward through perforators.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Why does the posterior tibial nerve remain vulnerable to entrapment in tarsal tunnel syndrome?
options: It passes through a fibro-osseous tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum behind the medial malleolus
It runs subcutaneously over the lateral malleolus
It winds around the neck of the fibula
questions.explanation: Compression of the tibial nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum in the tarsal tunnel causes burning pain and paresthesia over the sole of the foot (tarsal tunnel syndrome).
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which arteries participate in the genicular anastomosis around the knee joint?
options: Superior/inferior medial & lateral genicular branches of popliteal artery, descending genicular branch of femoral artery, descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral, and anterior tibial recurrent artery
questions.explanation: The rich genicular anastomosis around the patella and femoral/tibial condyles links the femoral, profunda femoris, popliteal, and anterior tibial arteries.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: In a patient with chronic occlusion of the superficial femoral artery in the adductor canal, which vessels serve as the primary collateral pathway to bypass the block and perfuse the lower leg?
options: Profunda femoris artery (via perforating and descending lateral circumflex branches) anastomosing with the genicular branches of the popliteal artery
questions.explanation: The profunda femoris acts as the critical collateral lifeline of the thigh, connecting proximally via the cruciate anastomosis and distally via the genicular anastomosis.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: A patient sustains a penetrating stab wound to the femoral triangle just lateral to the femoral artery. Which nerve is injured, and what motor deficit results?
options: Obturator nerve; loss of thigh adduction
Femoral nerve; paralysis of quadriceps femoris (loss of knee extension) and weakened hip flexion, with absent patellar reflex
Sciatic nerve; loss of knee flexion and foot drop
Common peroneal nerve; loss of foot eversion
questions.explanation: The femoral nerve lies immediately lateral to the femoral artery (outside the femoral sheath) in the femoral triangle; its injury paralyzes the quadriceps, abolishes knee extension and the patellar jerk, and causes sensory loss over the anterior thigh and medial leg.
questions.source: Dr. Khalid Milad — supplied question bank

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: The profunda femoris artery reaches the posterior compartment of the thigh by giving off which set of branches?
questions.explanation: The profunda femoris enters the medial compartment and sends four perforating branches to the posterior compartment.
questions.source: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.reference_snapshot: Profunda femoris sends four perforators posteriorly. PDF p. 48; slide 48

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which structure does the articular branch of the obturator artery enter to supply the head of the femur?
options: Ligament of the head of the femur (ligamentum teres)
questions.explanation: The articular branch enters the ligament of the head of the femur (ligamentum teres).
questions.source: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.reference_snapshot: Articular branch enters ligamentum teres and supplies femoral head. PDF p. 49; slide 49

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: During femoral hernia surgery, which arterial variant is highlighted as a potential source of dangerous bleeding near the lacunar ligament?
options: An inferior epigastric pubic branch replacing the obturator artery
A superficial circumflex iliac artery crossing the femoral ring
A descending genicular artery entering the femoral canal
A medial circumflex femoral artery crossing the inguinal ligament
questions.explanation: The pubic branch of the inferior epigastric artery may replace the obturator artery and descend in the free margin of the lacunar ligament.
questions.source: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.reference_snapshot: Inferior epigastric pubic branch may replace obturator and descend in lacunar ligament margin. PDF p. 50; slide 50

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which artery is listed as a branch of the popliteal artery that supplies the knee joint centrally?
questions.explanation: The popliteal artery branches include the middle genicular artery.
questions.source: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.reference_snapshot: Middle genicular artery listed among popliteal branches. PDF p. 52; slide 52

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: At the lower border of popliteus, which veins unite to form the popliteal vein?
options: Venae comitantes of the anterior and posterior tibial arteries
Anterior tibial and fibular veins only
questions.explanation: The lecture describes the popliteal vein as beginning at the lower border of popliteus by union of the venae comitantes of the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
questions.source: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.reference_snapshot: The slide locates the union at the lower border of popliteus and names the two venae comitantes. PDF p. 56; slide 56

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which pair of arteries contributes to the trochanteric anastomosis from the internal iliac system?
questions.explanation: The trochanteric anastomosis includes superior and inferior gluteal arteries, alongside medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries.
questions.source: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.reference_snapshot: Superior and inferior gluteal arteries are listed contributors. PDF p. 58; slide 58

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which artery contributes to the anastomosis around the anterior superior iliac spine from the external iliac system?
questions.explanation: The deep circumflex iliac artery is an external iliac contributor to the anastomosis around the ASIS.
questions.source: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.reference_snapshot: Deep circumflex iliac listed as external iliac contributor. PDF p. 60; slide 60

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which recurrent artery is listed as participating in the arterial anastomosis around the knee?
questions.explanation: The knee anastomosis list includes anterior and posterior tibial recurrent arteries.
questions.source: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.reference_snapshot: Posterior tibial recurrent artery appears in knee anastomosis list. PDF p. 61; slide 61

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which two cutaneous nerves are listed as branches of the anterior division of the femoral nerve?
options: Medial and intermediate cutaneous nerves of the thigh
Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh and saphenous nerve
Medial cutaneous nerve of thigh and deep peroneal nerve
questions.explanation: The anterior division gives medial and intermediate cutaneous nerves of the thigh.
questions.source: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.reference_snapshot: Anterior-division cutaneous branches are medial and intermediate thigh nerves. PDF p. 64; slide 64

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: After passing between sartorius and gracilis, the saphenous nerve descends along which side of the leg?
questions.explanation: The saphenous nerve becomes superficial between sartorius and gracilis and descends at the medial side of the knee and leg.
questions.source: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.reference_snapshot: Course is medial at knee and leg after becoming superficial. PDF p. 66; slide 66

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which knee-related branch is attributed to the posterior division of the obturator nerve?
options: An articular branch passing through the adductor hiatus
A cutaneous branch to the lateral calf
A saphenous branch accompanying the great saphenous vein
questions.explanation: The posterior division gives an articular branch to the knee, passing through the adductor hiatus.
questions.source: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.reference_snapshot: Posterior division articular branch reaches knee through hiatus. PDF p. 68; slide 68

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: In the gluteal region, which muscle is the sciatic nerve described as passing deep to as it leaves the region?
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve leaves the gluteal region by passing deep to the long head of biceps femoris.
questions.source: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.reference_snapshot: Sciatic nerve leaves gluteal region deep to biceps long head. PDF p. 70; slide 70

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which hamstring muscle is supplied through the common peroneal portion of the sciatic nerve rather than the tibial portion?
questions.explanation: The posterior thigh muscles are supplied through the tibial portion except the short head of biceps, supplied by the common peroneal portion.
questions.source: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.reference_snapshot: Short head of biceps is the stated exception. PDF p. 71; slide 71

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: As the tibial nerve runs with the posterior tibial artery in the leg, which sequence of positions relative to the artery is described?
questions.explanation: The lecture gives the tibial nerve’s relation to the posterior tibial artery as medial, then superficial, then lateral.
questions.source: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.reference_snapshot: The slide explicitly marks the sequence M → S → L alongside the posterior tibial artery. PDF p. 75; slide 75

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: Which cutaneous branch of the tibial nerve supplies the medial side of the heel?
questions.explanation: The medial calcaneal nerve is listed among tibial nerve cutaneous branches.
questions.source: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.reference_snapshot: Medial calcaneal nerve is listed as tibial cutaneous branch. PDF p. 76; slide 76

questions.subject: LL
questions.stem: A sensory deficit on the lateral side of the little toe most directly implicates which nerve?
questions.explanation: The sural nerve supplies the lateral side of the foot and lateral side of the fifth toe.
questions.source: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.reference_snapshot: Sural supplies lateral foot and lateral side of little toe. PDF p. 81; slide 81
